units: the person leading the group states that the moisture does not fall from the sky

text: The guide stops at the edge of the trail and tells her group to look at the flattened grass. Dew never falls from the sky, she says, whatever most walkers picture. Through the dark hours the ground gives up its heat to an open sky, and its surface ends up colder than the air resting against it. The moisture held in that air turns to tiny beads on the chilled blades. One woman in the group breaks in: she saw nothing of the kind the day before. Wind, the guide answers, kept stirring the air, so nothing had the chance to cool. Cloud works the same way, she adds, throwing the heat back down. And when a pale veil lingers in the hollow of the valley, that is the same process again, spread through a whole layer of air.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the growers of older generations could do nothing against the rising water

text: You are probably wondering what growers of older generations did when the river swelled. Not much. They took it. The flood tore out the seedlings, drowned the pens, and now and then carried off a whole storehouse. Then somebody noticed an odd thing: where the water had pulled back, the next harvest came in richer. The mud left behind fed the ground better than any animal manure. So the trick was to keep the fertility and skip the wreckage. The answer arrived piece by piece. They dug channels that steered the flood into shallow basins. They raised packed banks of clay along the shores. They cut gates that two men could open at the hour they chose. The water came in, dropped its load, and drained away on its own. Farming stopped being left to chance.

units: two agents shape the stones of a valley in different ways

this distinction makes it possible to rebuild the past of a slope with no clue left
text: Two agents shape the stones of a valley, and they do not go about it the same way. Running water rolls its blocks along, knocks them into one another, and wears them down by steady friction; what comes out is round, smooth, and sorted by size all down the course. Ice rolls nothing. It carries its load like a slow belt and drops it just as it was, so the fragments keep their cutting edges and lie jumbled together, a huge piece beside a smear of clay dust. A specialist tells the two deposits apart at a glance. Where water did the work, the grains match one another and settle in clean layers. Where ice passed, the sediment stays chaotic. That contrast lets you rebuild the past of a slope when nothing visible is left of it.

units: a child regularly brought back finds picked up in a wood

text: The child came back from the wood with her pockets sagging, and nobody ever knew what she would pull out. Feathers came first, laid in a row by shade, darkest to palest. Then the empty shells, so thin they cracked open in her palm. Then strips of bark, which she rubbed and held under her nose for the smell of resin and rain. A hard gust had brought down a beech in the cold season, and ever since she carried home splinters of pale wood torn from the split trunk. Last of all, right at the bottom, lay the stones: a streaked pebble, a lump of milky quartz, a piece of shale that peeled apart between her fingers. Her grandmother kept none of it. She lent a box, listened to the account of every piece, and waited for the next haul.

putting in a plant cover brings that value down
text: Start on an even slope with no thick cover growing on it, and mark off a square plot with stakes. Drive a metal border into the ground along three sides, so that it stands a hand's height above the surface. On the downhill side, fit a tilted trough that carries the water into a marked jug set in a pit. Now wait for a shower. The moment it stops, read off the volume you have caught, stir the contents, then draw a sample into a clean bottle. Let the mud settle overnight, pour off the clear water, dry the residue and weigh it. Write down the slope of the plot and the state of its surface. Repeat this after every shower and you will have the solid load the runoff carries away, and you will watch that figure drop as soon as plant cover takes hold.

text: A crack several paces long opened this week along the flank of a farmed plateau, forcing the authorities to close the track that runs across it. Geologists sent to survey the site put the opening down to a run of downpours well out of the ordinary. Water working its way underground has soaked a bed of clay buried beneath the fields; once saturated, that bed lost its grip, and the ground above it began to creep toward the bank. The movement, at first too slow to notice, picked up speed when a poorly drained retaining wall gave way. The farmers now fear for the spring that waters their livestock, since the fissure is turning aside part of the underground flow. Instruments will be put in before the wet season to follow how far the break advances.

text: Past a low bridge the river runs into a shoulder of rock and swings sharply aside. A standing whirlpool has dug itself in there, dark at the center, ringed with brown foam. On the inside of the bend fine sand keeps building up, while the outer bank gives back about the width of a hand every rainy season. The alder roots end up hanging in open air, and once a rise in the water strips them, the tree goes over. The people living along the river ruled out pouring concrete on the bank. They drove living willow stakes in at a slant where the water bites hardest, then wove supple branches between them. The wood takes hold, the roots stitch the soil together, and the current loses its force among the drowned leaves. The whirlpool remains, but it now digs the bed instead of eating the bank.

units: the writer invites the reader to set two ways of handling a river side by side

text: Honestly, we would do well to set two ways of handling a river side by side before picking ours. The first boxes it in: straighten the bed, harden the banks, raise the levees another notch at every warning. That works, right up to the moment it stops working, and then the water goes all at once, faster and higher than it ever would have without us. The second way looks far less impressive. You hand the river back its floodable meadows, pull the works back, and accept that fields with nobody on them will go under. The water spreads, slows, and drops its silt where it enriches instead of wrecking. I know the second choice means giving up land you own, and giving up has never pleased anyone. But the first commits us to raising the stakes forever, and its bill lands at the worst possible moment.

text: Nothing marked out a boatman's daughter to become the hydrologist that the keepers of dams now call on. Her working life falls into three parts. There is the field first: she spent whole seasons scooping muddy water out of the middle of the current, slung in a cradle above it, to weigh what the river was carrying off. Then the laboratory, where she worked out a way of sorting grains so cheap that far-off teams with no money for equipment took it up. Last comes the passing on: every season she takes in beginners and sends them wading through the silt long before she opens a manual for them. Those close to her describe a blunt woman, sparing with praise, and quite unable to turn down a call at night when a bank threatens to give.

text: The exhibition opens in a room with almost no light, and the choice makes sense from the doorway, because you listen before you see. A gale turns around you while the shadows of clouds slide across the floor. The second room lights its cases at last: cores of sediment standing upright like columns, layered in pale and dark bands that tell of dry seasons and wet ones. After that comes a more instructive gallery, the weakest stretch by far, where too many panels repeat what the objects had already said better. The last room makes up for everything. A wall of wet clay, lit from the side, dries as you watch and splits open during the visit; the cracking carries in the quiet. You come out feeling you have seen matter grow old, which no photograph could have given you.
